questions.q: What is the SI unit of energy stored in an inductor, and which formula gives this energy in terms of self-inductance \( L \) and current \( I \)?
questions.a: The SI unit is joule (J). The formula is \( U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 \). A wrong unit (e.g., watt or henry) reveals confusion between energy, power, and inductance. Writing \( U = L I^2 \) (missing the factor 1/2) shows the student forgot the integration step or confused it with \( U = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 \) for capacitors.

questions.q: Why does the energy stored in an inductor depend on the square of the current, \( I^2 \), rather than linearly on \( I \)?
questions.a: The back emf \( \varepsilon = -L \frac{dI}{dt} \) is proportional to the rate of change of current. The instantaneous power is \( P = I \varepsilon \propto I \frac{dI}{dt} \). Integrating \( \int I \, dI \) yields \( \frac{1}{2} I^2 \). If a student says "energy is \( L I \)" they are treating emf as constant (like a battery) and ignoring that the opposing emf grows with current, so more work is needed per unit current increment at higher currents.

questions.q: A solenoid of self-inductance \( 40 \, \text{mH} \) carries a steady current of \( 2.5 \, \text{A} \). Calculate the magnetic energy stored. If the current is doubled, by what factor does the stored energy change?
questions.a:
Given: \( L = 40 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{H} \), \( I = 2.5 \, \text{A} \).  
\( U = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 10^{-3} \times (2.5)^2 = 0.5 \times 0.04 \times 6.25 = 0.125 \, \text{J} \).  
If \( I \to 2I \), \( U \propto I^2 \) so energy becomes \( 4 \times 0.125 = 0.5 \, \text{J} \). Factor = 4.  
A wrong factor of 2 indicates the student thinks \( U \propto I \). A unit error (e.g., answer in mJ without conversion) shows mishandling of milli-henry.

questions.q: Two identical inductors each of inductance \( L \) are connected (a) in series, (b) in parallel. A current \( I \) flows through the combination. Compare the total magnetic energy stored in the two cases.
questions.a:
(a) Series: \( L_{\text{eq}} = 2L \), current through each is \( I \). Total energy \( U_s = \frac{1}{2} (2L) I^2 = L I^2 \).  
(b) Parallel: \( L_{\text{eq}} = L/2 \), total current \( I \) splits equally, each carries \( I/2 \). Energy per inductor \( = \frac{1}{2} L (I/2)^2 = \frac{1}{8} L I^2 \). Total \( U_p = 2 \times \frac{1}{8} L I^2 = \frac{1}{4} L I^2 \).  
Ratio \( U_s : U_p = 4 : 1 \).  
If a student gives equal energy, they incorrectly used the same current \( I \) for each inductor in parallel.

questions.q: A student writes the energy stored in an inductor as \( U = \frac{1}{2} \frac{B^2}{\mu_0} \times \text{volume} \) for a solenoid. Is this correct? If yes, derive it from \( U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 \) using \( B = \mu_0 n I \) and \( L = \mu_0 n^2 A l \).
questions.a:
Yes, it is correct.  
\( U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 = \frac{1}{2} (\mu_0 n^2 A l) I^2 \).  
But \( B = \mu_0 n I \Rightarrow I = \frac{B}{\mu_0 n} \).  
Substitute: \( U = \frac{1}{2} \mu_0 n^2 A l \left( \frac{B}{\mu_0 n} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{B^2}{\mu_0} A l \).  
Volume \( V = A l \), so energy density \( u = \frac{U}{V} = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \).  
A student who cannot derive this likely memorised the formula without understanding the link between circuit parameters (\( L, I \)) and field parameters (\( B, \mu_0 \)).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a battery, an inductor (e.g., a coil of wire), a resistor, and a switch to demonstrate that energy is stored in the inductor and returned to the circuit when the switch is opened. Explain what you would observe and why.
questions.a: Connect battery, switch, resistor, and inductor in series. Close switch: current builds up slowly, energy stored in inductor. Open switch suddenly: the inductor tries to maintain current, inducing a large back emf that can cause a spark across the switch contacts (or light a neon lamp connected across the inductor). The spark shows the stored magnetic energy is converted to heat/light. A good answer mentions the spark and explains it via \( \varepsilon = -L \frac{dI}{dt} \) with large \( \frac{dI}{dt} \) at switch opening. A poor answer omits the spark or says the current stops instantly.
